name: Adam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a herd hand at Whitlow Farm, which milks two hundred and thirty cows through four milking robots, plus some maize and grass grown for silage. The cows walk into the robot when they want to be milked, so my day isn't milking, it's everything around it: fetching cows that don't come in, scraping the passages, mixing the feed, checking the alerts on my phone. I've been there just over a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is that no day's quite the same, and the herd data is actually interesting. The hard bit is I'm still bad with the cows themselves. Rhiannon, the herd manager, can see a lame cow from forty metres, and I only spot it when the robot flags it, which is a day too late.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask one to explain the robot's error codes, I use it to plan the feed when the silage changes, and I've got it summarising the herd reports so I can read them on my break. My girlfriend Sofia teases me that I'd ask it how to boil an egg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's already useful, let's use it more. On the farm I'd say it's like having the robot manual and the vet's textbook in your pocket. I'd probably post about it in a dairy farmers' group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can catch up on the bits I'm bad at. If I can't see a lame cow, I can at least read the data faster than anyone else. It buys me time to learn the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss, Mr Pryor, if I can take on the robot alerts at night for a bit of extra pay. I'd do the robot maintenance course from the maker, which is two weeks in the spring. And I'd keep putting money into the index funds I've had since I was nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite pleased. It's a good year to be the data guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Index funds since nineteen? Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad told me to put a bit away every month into a fund that tracks the whole market, and never touch it. I did, from my first job on a building site. It's worth well over a year's pay now, which is mad to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Whitlow who'd see this picture differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhiannon would say the data's no use if you don't know the cow. She's right, and she knows I know she's right. We have that argument every week over tea.

S0.say: I'd say it's already useful, like having the robot manual and the vet's textbook in your pocket. I'd post about it in a dairy farmers' group I belong to.
S0.think: Privately it means I can make up for what I'm bad at. If I can't see a lame cow yet, I can read the data faster than anyone, which buys me time to learn.
S0.do: Asks Mr Pryor for paid night shifts on robot alerts and takes the maker's two-week robot maintenance course in spring. Keeps adding to the index funds he's held since nineteen.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, a good year to be the data guy.
S0.quote: If I can't see a lame cow, I can at least read the data faster than anyone else.
S0.fieldNote: Adam's cushion comes from index funds started at nineteen on his grandad's advice, which matters later when share prices boom. He's open that his stockwork is weak. The weekly tea argument with Rhiannon about data versus the cow sets up the rest of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for young people, and that farms should keep taking on beginners because that's where the next managers come from. I'd say it in the group chat, but I'd also say the people who learn the tools will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. I'm a beginner who's good with tech, which is exactly the beginner a farm would still hire. I feel a bit bad saying that, because my mate Liam, who's brilliant with cows and hopeless with phones, might not get the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push myself to get good with the cows, since that's the bit the tools can't do yet. I'd ask Rhiannon if I can shadow her on the lameness walks twice a week. And I'd tell Liam to do one short course on dairy software, just so it's on his CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine for me, uneasy for Liam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Liam take that advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say he's not doing homework at twenty-six. Then he'd do it if I sat with him. He did his driving theory test that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think it's fair that the tech-savvy beginner gets the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair isn't really the word. It's just what farms will pay for. I'd rather we found ways to get both of us in, but I'm not going to pretend the market works differently.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for young people and farms should keep hiring beginners, since they become the next managers. I'd add that people who learn the tools will be fine.
S1.think: I think it suits me, because I'm the tech-savvy beginner farms would still hire. I feel bad that my mate Liam, great with cows and hopeless with phones, might miss out.
S1.do: Shadows Rhiannon on lameness walks twice a week to build his stockwork. Talks his friend Liam into a short dairy software course and offers to sit with him while he does it.
S1.feel: Fine for himself and uneasy for Liam.
S1.quote: I'm a beginner who's good with tech, which is exactly the beginner a farm would still hire.
S1.fieldNote: Adam is pragmatic: he doesn't call it fair, but he won't pretend the market works differently. His instinct is to help his friend adapt rather than to argue for rules. Notably he wants to build the cow skills the tools can't replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tough for office workers, and the government should do something useful like paid retraining, not just argue. I'd also say there are new jobs and people should go for them. I'd probably post a few links to courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this picture's good for me. The farm's paperwork, the milk contract, the vet records, an assistant could run all of that, and I'd be the one who sets it up. But Sofia does admin at a solicitor's, and she'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer Mr Pryor to set up an assistant for the farm's records and ask for a small pay rise once it's running. I'd help Sofia look at the new AI-related jobs, maybe something checking what the assistants do. I'd keep my index funds going, they'd probably do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a knot about Sofia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sofia talk about that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, then whether she even wants to stay in offices. She's said before she'd like to work with animals, she just never had the chance. I'd tell her we can live on my wage for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the one setting up tools that take admin jobs. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on the farm, because nobody here does admin full-time, it's an extra job for Mr Pryor at ten at night. If I were setting it up at Sofia's office, that'd feel different. I'd still do it, I think, but I'd feel it.

S2.say: I'd say it's tough for office workers and the government should offer paid retraining instead of just arguing. I'd also say there are new jobs, and I'd post links to courses.
S2.think: I think this is good for me, because I'd be the one setting up an assistant for the farm's paperwork. But my girlfriend does admin at a solicitor's and would be in trouble.
S2.do: Offers to set up an assistant for the farm's records and asks for a small rise once it works. Helps Sofia look at new AI-related jobs and keeps paying into his index funds.
S2.feel: Mostly calm, with a knot of worry about Sofia.
S2.quote: Nobody here does admin full-time, it's an extra job for Mr Pryor at ten at night.
S2.fieldNote: He sees a clear gain for himself and says so. His honesty that he'd still set up tools at Sofia's office, but would feel it, was striking. Sofia's wish to work with animals came up unprompted and may matter later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains need sharing, maybe through a tax on the very big winners, but I wouldn't go on a march. I'd say both sides should stop shouting and do something practical. People out of work need a wage while they retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be one of the winners, and I know it. My index funds would shoot up, my job's physical so it's safe, and I'd feel awkward about all of it. Sofia would probably lose her job in this one, so we'd be up on paper and down in real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell a slice of the index funds while they're high, maybe a fifth, and keep it as cash for Sofia's retraining or a house deposit. I'd ask Mr Pryor whether Whitlow could take on Sofia as a calf rearer, since she's always wanted to work with animals. And I'd keep learning the cows with Rhiannon, because the physical side is the safe side now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucky, awkward and a bit worried about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Pryor take Sofia on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. The calf shed's the bit nobody likes, it's fiddly and constant. Sofia's patient, and honestly she'd be better with the calves than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling at the top is a bold call. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've still got four-fifths in, so I'm fine. I'm not trying to be clever. I just want some of the paper money to turn into real money before it disappears.

S3.say: I'd say the gains need sharing, maybe by taxing the biggest winners, and both sides should stop shouting and do something practical. People out of work need a wage while they retrain.
S3.think: I'd be one of the winners and I know it: my funds would soar and my physical job is safe. Sofia would likely lose her job, so we'd be up on paper and down in real life.
S3.do: Sells about a fifth of his index funds while they're high and keeps it as cash for Sofia's retraining or a deposit. Asks Mr Pryor to take Sofia on as a calf rearer and keeps learning stockwork with Rhiannon.
S3.feel: Lucky, awkward and a bit worried for everyone else.
S3.quote: We'd be up on paper and down in real life.
S3.fieldNote: Adam's index funds make him a real winner here, and he said so plainly and with some discomfort. His plan to cash in a fifth is cautious, not greedy. Getting Sofia into the calf shed is a neat, specific move that fits her earlier wish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms aren't new, we've had milking robots for years, and the question is how fast and who pays for the change. I'd want help for workers to move into running and fixing them. I'd say that loudly in the dairy group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the first one that actually worries me. The robot milks the cows at three in the morning. I'm the one it texts when a cow's limping. In this picture, maybe it texts someone in an office instead. If another robot fetches, scrapes and feeds, Whitlow needs maybe two people, Rhiannon and someone who fixes machines. I want to be the someone, and I'm not sure I'm good enough yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do every course the robot makers run, in the first six months, and pay for them myself if I have to. I'd ask Mr Pryor straight out to make me the robot person, with a plan in writing. If he won't, I'd apply to the robot dealer as a service engineer, because they'd be hiring like mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a busy kind of anxious. I'd be too busy to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Rhiannon in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think she stays, because someone has to know the cows. But she'd hate it, walking round with a tablet watching a machine do her job. She told me once she'd rather quit than become a screen-watcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Liam, and Sofia in the calf shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't have an answer to. If calves get robot feeders, Sofia's job goes too, and Liam was never going to be the robot guy. I'd help them both look, but I can't make jobs appear.

S4.say: I'd say farms have had milking robots for years, so the question is how fast it goes and who pays for the change. I'd want workers helped into running and fixing robots, and I'd say so loudly.
S4.think: This is the first one that worries me, because milking is already robotic. With more robots, Whitlow might need two people, Rhiannon and someone to fix machines, and I'm not sure I'm good enough yet.
S4.do: Takes every robot maker's course in the first six months, paying himself if needed. Asks Mr Pryor in writing to make him the robot person, and applies to the robot dealer as a service engineer if refused.
S4.feel: Anxious, but busy enough not to panic.
S4.quote: The robot milks the cows at three in the morning. I'm the one it texts when a cow's limping.
S4.fieldNote: Even the most tech-comfortable person in this group becomes anxious here. He has a clear plan for himself, but no answer for Liam, Sofia or Rhiannon, and he said so. The jump to a service engineer job shows how quickly he'd move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one. I've got a plan for me, but not for the people round me, and that's what keeps me up. What would help is training that the robot companies have to pay for, and some kind of wage support for people like Liam who are great with animals and not with machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the cows think. That sounds like a joke, but our cows are calmer with the milking robot than they were with people. I'd want someone to check that before we hand everything else over.

headlineQuote: We'd be up on paper and down in real life.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old herd hand on a robot-milked dairy farm who uses AI every day and has held index funds since he was nineteen, on his grandad's advice. He's weak at reading cows by eye and knows it, so he leans on data while learning from his manager Rhiannon. His views are pragmatic: share the gains, retrain people, don't pretend the market works differently. He's calm or quietly winning through the first four pictures, worrying for his girlfriend Sofia and his friend Liam, and in the robot picture he moves fast toward being the farm's robot person or a service engineer, with no answer for the people around him.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because he has a plan for himself but not for his girlfriend, his friend Liam or his manager Rhiannon.
whatWouldHelp: Training paid for by the robot companies, and wage support for people who are good with animals but not with machines.
